text: You could add 40, ten times.
That works. But it takes a while, and it's easy to lose count.
Is there a faster way? Yes. It's in this chart of places.
Slide a digit left and it's worth 10 times as much, slide it right and it's worth one tenth as much.
Look at the places, from the right.
10 ones make 1 ten. 10 tens make 1 hundred. 10 hundreds make 1 thousand.
See the pattern? Each step to the left is 10 times as much.
Look at 40. The 4 is in the tens place.
Slide it one place to the left, into the hundreds. That's 400.
That's 10 times as much. So a carton holds 400 pencils.
Now go back the other way. One box is one tenth of a carton.
Slide the 4 in 400 one place to the right, back to the tens. That's 40.
So one tenth of 400 is 40 pencils.
Here's the part people mix up.

text: Add 37 one thousand times? That would take all day.
There's a faster way. And it works for dividing too.
Each zero in 10, 100 or 1,000 slides every digit one place, left to multiply and right to divide.
Start with 10. It has one zero.
So 37 times 10 slides the 3 and the 7 one place to the left.
The ones place is empty now, so a zero fills it. That's 370.
Now 100. It has two zeros, so the digits slide two places. That's 3,700.
1,000 has three zeros, so they slide three places. That's 37,000.
So the shop has 37,000 beads.
Now go backwards. The shop shares 37,000 beads into 1,000 bags.
1,000 still has three zeros. So every digit slides three places — this time to the right.
The zeros slide off the end. That's 37 beads in each bag.
When you divide, don't slide left.
Dividing makes the number smaller, so every digit slides right.
Six zeros in a row are hard to count at a glance. Try it.
And if you write one zero too many, the number is 10 times too big.
The small number up top says how many 10s to multiply.
That is how many zeros, and how many places the digits slide.
Let us count them together. 10 times 10 is two 10s, so we write 10 squared.
And 10 times 10 times 10 is three 10s, so we write 10 cubed.
Watch the last column. Each 10 you multiply adds one zero.
Back to our city. 1,000,000 is a 1 with 6 zeros. Count them with me.
Six zeros means six 10s multiplied, so the city has 10⁶ people.
Here is the part I really like.
That small number also tells you how many places the digits slide.
So 45 times 10 cubed slides them 3 places left, and 62,000 divided by 10 cubed slides them 3 places right.
Careful with this one.
Do not multiply 10 by the small number. 10 cubed is not 10 times 3.
It means three 10s multiplied together.
Working out 28 times 412 exactly takes a lot of steps.
But sometimes you do not need exact. You only need to know about how many.
Is it near 1,000? Near 10,000? Near 100,000?
Swap each number for a close round number.
Use a fact you know, then write the zeros.
Round each number at its biggest place.
28 is only 2 away from 30. Look how close that is.
And 412 is only 12 away from 400.
So 28 times 412 is close to 30 times 400.
Now use a fact you already know. 3 times 4 equals 12.
Then count the zeros. 30 has one and 400 has two, so three zeros go after the 12.
12,000. The farm packs about 12,000 eggs.
Dividing works the very same way. 2,380 eggs go into crates of 58.
Round 58 to the nearest ten, 60, and round 2,380 to the nearest hundred, 2,400.
24 divided by 6 equals 4, and 60 times 40 equals 2,400. So it is about 40 crates.
Last one, and it is the slip that costs the most.
Do not lose the zeros.
30 has one zero and 400 has two, so the answer needs three zeros after the 12.
A kilometer is a long way. You could walk it, but it would take you a while.
A meter? That is about one big step.
So the run is only 5 kilometers, but it is going to be a lot of meters.
A bigger unit is made of 10, 100 or 1,000 smaller ones.
Multiply to change to the smaller unit, and divide to change to the bigger one.
The kilometer is the bigger unit here.
And 1 kilometers is exactly the same length as 1,000 meters.
So every single kilometer of that run is 1,000 meters.
Meters are smaller, so it takes more of them to cover the same distance.
Smaller unit, more of them. That means we multiply.
5 times 1,000 equals 5,000, the same sliding you already know. So the run is 5,000 meters long.
Now, a runner has gone 3,000 meters so far.
Kilometers are bigger, so there are fewer of them. Fewer of them means we go the other way, and divide.
3,000 divided by 1,000 equals 3. That runner has gone 3 kilometers.
Here is the one that catches people.
When you change to the bigger unit, don't multiply.
A kilogram (kg) is 1,000 grams (g), so 6,000 grams is only 6 kilograms. A much smaller number.
Look carefully at the two numbers. The jug is measured in liters, but the cups are in milliliters.
The 2 and the 250 count different units, so we cannot divide them yet.
Change to the same unit first.
Then solve the story one step at a time.
1 liters is 1,000 milliliters, so let us count that jug in milliliters.
The jug holds 2 times 1,000 equals 2,000 milliliters.
Now the jug and the cups are both in milliliters.
Now the cups. 4 cups of 250 milliliters make 1,000 milliliters.
The jug holds two of those thousands, so 2 times 4 equals 8 cups.
And that is exactly what 2,000 divided by 250 asks.
Always check. 8 cups of 250 milliliters is 8 times 250 equals 2,000 milliliters.
That is 2 liters, the whole jug, with nothing left over.
You can fill 8 cups.
Here is the one to avoid.
Do not do the math with two different units.
Change 2 liters into 2,000 milliliters first, and then divide.
6 times 128 is not a fact you know by heart, is it?
And adding 128 six times takes a long time, where one slip changes the answer.
Break the big number into hundreds, tens and ones.
Multiply each part, then add all the parts.
128 is 1 hundred, 2 tens and 8 ones.
So split each row of 128 into three parts, 100, 20 and 8.
Now take them one at a time. 6 times 1 hundred is 6 hundreds, so 6 times 100 equals 600.
6 times 2 tens is 12 tens, so 6 times 20 equals 120.
And 6 times 8 equals 48.
Last move. Add the three parts, 600 plus 120 plus 48 equals 768.
So 6 times 128 equals 768. There are 768 corn plants in the field.
Watch this one.
Do not multiply the digits as if they were all ones.
The 1 in 128 means 100 and the 2 means 20, so the parts are 600 and 120, not 6 and 12.
You can already multiply 115 by one digit.
But 26 has two digits, and adding 115 twenty-six times would take far too long.
Break the two-digit number into tens and ones.
Multiply by each part, then add the two answers.
26 is 2 tens and 6 ones.
So 26 boxes are 20 boxes and 6 more boxes, and each box still holds 115 books.
Start with the easy piece. 115 times 2 equals 230.
20 is 10 times 2, so 115 times 20 is 10 times as much, 2,300.
Then the ones, 115 times 6 equals 690.
Now add the two answers, 2,300 plus 690 equals 2,990.
So 115 times 26 equals 2,990. The shop gets 2,990 books.
Here is the slip to avoid.
Do not multiply by 2 when the 2 is in the tens place.
It means 2 tens, which is 20. So multiply 115 by 20, not by 2.
Breaking 23 into 20 and 3 works just fine.
But writing out 124 times 20 and 124 times 3 takes a lot of space.
Columns do the same work with much less writing.
Multiply by the ones, then write a 0 and multiply by the tens.
Add the two rows.
First row first. Multiply 124 by the 3 ones.
4 times 3 equals 12, so write the 2 and carry the 1.
2 times 3 equals 6, plus the carried 1 makes 7. And 1 times 3 equals 3. The first row is 372.
Now the 2 in 23. It is not 2, it is 2 tens.
So write a 0 in the ones place first, to hold it there.
Then 124 times 2 equals 248, and the second row is 2,480.
Now add them. 372 plus 2,480 equals 2,852.
And look, those rows are 124 times 3 and 124 times 20, the same two parts as breaking 23 apart.
There are 2,852 chairs in the hall.
This is the one almost everybody trips on.
Do not forget the 0 when you multiply by the tens.
Without it, the second row is only 248 instead of 2,480.
For a two-digit number you made two rows, the ones and the tens.
But 123 has three digits, so there are hundreds to deal with too.
Make one row for each digit of the bottom number, and start each new row with one more 0.
Then add all the rows.
Start with the 3 ones, 231 times 3.
1 times 3 equals 3, 3 times 3 equals 9 and 2 times 3 equals 6. The first row is 693.
Next the 2 in 123. That 2 means 2 tens, so write one 0 first.
Then 231 times 2 equals 462, and the second row is 4,620.
Last row. The 1 in 123 means 1 hundred, so this time write two 0s first.
Then 231 times 1 equals 231, and the row is 23,100.
Add all three rows, 693 plus 4,620 plus 23,100 equals 28,413 bottles.
Careful right at the end.
Do not forget the two 0s in the hundreds row.
The 1 in 123 means 1 hundred, so that row is 23,100, not 231.
You can already multiply 406 times 35 the standard way.
But with big numbers, one small slip, like a lost 0, can throw the answer a long way off.
And the worst part is that it still looks like a real answer.
Estimate first with round numbers.
Then multiply the standard way and check that your answer is close.
Round each number to its biggest place. 406 rounds to 400, and 35 rounds to 40.
400 times 40 equals 16,000, so our answer should land somewhere close to 16,000.
Now the real thing. The ones row is 406 times 5 equals 2,030.
For the tens row, write a 0 first, then 406 times 3 equals 1,218. The row is 12,180.
Add them, 2,030 plus 12,180 equals 14,210.
Now the check. That is close to 16,000, so the answer makes sense.
The warehouse ships 14,210 toys.
And here is what the estimate is for.
Do not keep an answer that is far from your estimate.
3,248 is nowhere near 16,000, because the tens row lost its 0. Look again and fix that row.
240 divided by 60 is not one of the facts you learned.
Counting up by 60s all the way to 240 is slow, and one slip changes the answer.
Think in tens.
240 is 24 tens and 60 is 6 tens, so 240 divided by 60 is the same as 24 divided by 6.
Each small step on this line is 10.
Jump 10 tens to 100, 10 more tens to 200, then 4 tens to 240.
Count them all up, and that is 24 tens.
Now one bus. It seats 60 students.
60 is 6 small steps, so it is 6 tens.
One busload is one jump of 6 tens.
So jump 6 tens at a time, all the way from 0 to 240.
It takes 4 jumps, because 24 divided by 6 equals 4.
So 240 divided by 60 equals 4. The students fill 4 buses.
One warning before you go.
Do not take the 0 off only one number.
That turns 240 divided by 60 into 240 divided by 6. Think of both numbers in tens.
You learned your facts up to 10 times 10, but nobody learns the 17s.
And counting 17, 34, 51 and on is slow, and it is hard to keep track.
Round the number you divide by to the nearest ten and make a guess.
Multiply to check, if a whole group still fits in what is left, the guess was too small.
17 is close to 20, so let us guess with 20s.
How many 20s fit into 68? 3 times 20 equals 60, and 4 times 20 equals 80 is too many.
So our guess is 3 teams.
Now check with the real team size, 3 times 17 equals 51.
Take it away, 68 minus 51 equals 17. There are 17 kids left.
Wait. 17 kids left is a whole team, so the guess was too small.
Add one more team, 4 times 17 equals 68, with no one left out.
So 68 divided by 17 equals 4. The coach makes 4 teams.
Here is the mistake to watch for.
Do not stop while a whole group still fits in what is left.
17 kids left make one more team of 17.
You usually start dividing with the first digit, or the first two.
But 23 does not fit into 1, and it does not fit into 18 either.
If the number you divide by does not fit into the first two digits, the answer has one digit.
Guess with round numbers, and if the guess is too big, try one less.
23 does not fit into 18 tens, so the answer has no tens at all.
It has just one digit, and that digit goes up over the 4.
23 is close to 20, so guess with 20s. How many 20s fit into 184?
9 times 20 equals 180, so guess 9.
Now check with the real number, 9 times 23 equals 207. That is more than 184, so 9 is too big.
So try one less. 8 times 23 equals 184.
It fits exactly, with 0 left. Write the 8 over the 4.
So 184 divided by 23 equals 8. The shop makes 8 bunches.
Here is the one to watch.
